text: The Darwin Medal is awarded by the Royal Society for "distinction in evolution, biological diversity and developmental, population and organismal biology." In 1885, the International Darwin Memorial Fund was transferred to the Royal Society and was established to promote biological research, ultimately leading to the creation of the Darwin Medal. The medal was first awarded in 1890 to Alfred Russel Wallace for "his independent origination of the theory of the origin of species by natural selection." It commemorates the work of English biologist Charles Darwin (1809–1882), best known for his 1859 book On the Origin of Species, who was a fellow of the Royal Society and had previously received the Royal Medal in 1853 and the Copley Medal in 1864. The medal has a diameter of 2+1⁄4 inch (5.7 cm) and is made of silver; its obverse features Darwin's portrait, while the reverse displays a wreath of plants with his name in Latin, "Carolus Darwin," surrounded by the years of his birth and death in Roman numerals (MDCCCIX and MDCCCLXXXII). The design was created by John Evans, president of the Royal Numismatic Society. Since its inception, the medal has been awarded over 60 times, including to Francis Darwin, Charles Darwin's son, and two married couples: Jack and Yolande Heslop-Harrison in 1982 and Peter and Rosemary Grant in 2002. Initially accompanied by a grant of £100, the medal is now awarded with a grant of £2,000. Eligibility is restricted to citizens who have resided in the United Kingdom, Commonwealth of Nations, or the Republic of Ireland for more than three years. The medal was awarded biennially from 1890 until 2018; since then, it has been awarded annually.
